stimulus.text:
“Article II. Each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence, and every power, jurisdiction, and right, which is not by this Confederation expressly delegated to the United States, in Congress assembled.
Article III. The said States hereby severally enter into a firm league of friendship with each other, for their common defence, the security of their liberties, and their mutual and general welfare, binding themselves to assist each other, against all force offered to, or attacks made upon them, or any of them, on account of religion, sovereignty, trade, or any other pretence whatever.”
— Articles of Confederation, adopted by Congress November 15, 1777 (in force March 1, 1781)

stem: According to Article II, a power that the Articles did NOT expressly give to Congress belonged to

options.misconception: Background: the Articles created no president and no executive branch at all.
Background: the Articles created no national court system.
Article II gives undelegated powers to the states, not to voters directly.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Article II says every power not expressly delegated to Congress stays with the states, so an undelegated power belonged to each state.
rationales.B: Background: no president existed under the Articles; there was no executive branch to hold powers.
rationales.C: Background: no national courts existed under the Articles; disputes stayed with the states.
rationales.D: Article II names the states, not the voters, as the holders of powers not delegated to Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Read what Article II keeps. Every power not expressly delegated stays with the states.
2. Background: the Articles gave Congress only a short list of powers, such as war and treaties.
3. Background: anything missing from that list, like taxing citizens, stayed with each state.
4. So an undelegated power never left the state that held it in the first place.
Remember: under the Articles, Congress held only what the states expressly gave it.
